vignette:
Patient Name: Elena M.
Age: 19
Occupation: Train Conductor
Date of Intake Notes: Session 4

Elena sits forward on the couch, her hands wrapped around a cold coffee cup she hasn't touched in twenty minutes. She is small-framed, with dark hair pulled into a tight ponytail that reveals the fine lines around her eyes-lines that seem out of place on a nineteen-year-old. She speaks in short bursts, her voice flat, as though she is reading a manual aloud.

"I don't remember a time before it," she says, without looking up. "The yelling. The breaking things. My mother's crying."

Elena grew up in a small apartment in a working-class neighborhood. Her father worked construction when he worked at all. Her mother cleaned houses. The violence started before Elena can remember-a push, a slap, a door slammed so hard the frame splintered. By the time she was six, she had learned to read the air in the room the way sailors read clouds. A certain tilt of her father's head. The way his voice dropped low and quiet. She would retreat to her closet, press her back against the wall, and count the seconds until the sound of a fist hitting flesh stopped.

She never told anyone. Not her teachers, not her friends, not the priest at the church her mother dragged her to every Sunday. "What happens in this house stays in this house," her mother would whisper afterward, pressing a cold washcloth to her own swollen lip. Elena learned to make herself small. Invisible. A ghost in her own home.

At sixteen, she got a job at a regional rail yard, sweeping floors and cleaning break rooms. It was loud. The screech of metal on metal, the hiss of air brakes, the constant clatter of freight cars coupling. She found it soothing. The noise was predictable. She could track each sound to its source. Unlike the sounds of her childhood-unexpected, violent, always just around the corner.

When she turned eighteen, she applied to be a conductor. The exam was rigorous. She passed easily. She had always been good at memorizing schedules, reading signals, staying calm under pressure. Her supervisors praised her focus. "Cool as a cucumber," one of them said. Elena didn't tell them that her calm was a survival skill, honed over years of standing perfectly still while glass shattered in the next room.

Now she works the overnight freight runs, three times a week. She loves the dark. The isolation. The way the train moves through the night like a secret. But lately, the noise has started to change.

It began six months ago, after a minor derailment on a siding. No one was hurt, but the impact was sharp, sudden. The car jolted. Metal screamed. For a moment, Elena was back in the closet, age seven, her hands over her ears. Her heart hammered so hard she thought she might vomit. She stood frozen in the cab, unable to move, while the engineer called her name over the radio. She didn't answer for a full minute.

Since then, the world has become a minefield. A dropped clipboard in the yard makes her flinch. A coworker shouting across the platform sends her heart into a sprint. She has started checking the locks on her apartment door three times before she can sleep. She sleeps only four hours a night, if that. Her dreams are not of trains. They are of the apartment. The closet. The sound of her mother's muffled sobs.

She has stopped seeing friends. She has stopped answering her phone. At work, she is still reliable, still punctual, but the other conductors have noticed she no longer eats lunch in the break room. She eats alone in the cab, facing the door.

"I don't know what's wrong with me," she says, finally looking up. Her eyes are dry, but her hands are shaking. "I got out. I got away. Why can't I just leave it behind?"

She does not mention the flashbacks. She does not mention the way she sometimes sees her father's face in the reflection of the train window, even though he has been dead for two years. She does not mention the way she has started wearing a heavy winter coat to work, even in summer, because the weight on her shoulders makes her feel less exposed.

She just sits there, in the quiet of the office, waiting for something to break.
